h1: SEO for breweries: getting found by drinkers searching nearby
title: SEO for Breweries | Craft Beer School
desc: A practical SEO guide for breweries: what to fix on your site this month, how local search works for a taproom and what not to promise yourself.
teaser: Nobody can promise you a ranking. You can make your site easy to find, easy to read and clearly about the right place.
standfirst: Search engine optimisation is a set of habits that help the right people find your brewery when they look. Most of the gains for a small brewery come from basics done carefully.
sections: What SEO can and cannot do

SEO is the work of making your pages easy for search engines to understand and useful to the person who lands on them. It does not give you control over rankings. Search engines decide. They change how they decide. Anyone who guarantees a position on page one is selling something you should not buy.

What you can do is remove obstacles and provide the best answer to the questions people ask. For a brewery, the main questions are local: where is it, when is it open, what is on tap and can I book.
The searches that matter for a brewery

Think in three groups. Local searches, such as a taproom near me or a brewery in your area, bring walk-in visitors. Brand searches, which are people typing your name, bring buyers who already know you. Topic searches, such as how a style tastes or what to pair with a beer, bring people early in their interest.

For most breweries local comes first, because it leads to visits and sales. Start there. Build the others over time. Our keyword research guide shows how to find the words people really use.
Fix the basics on your site first

• Each page has one clear topic, a title that says what it is and a short description written for people.
  • Your address, opening hours and phone number are written as text on the page, not only inside an image.
  • The site loads quickly on a phone, since most visitors arrive on one.
  • Every beer has its own page with style, strength and tasting notes.
  • An events page and a booking route that works.
  • A sitemap submitted through Google Search Console, which is free.

If you run an age gate, check that it does not hide your content from search engines. Ask your web developer to test how the page looks to a crawler.

For a taproom, your free Google Business Profile often matters as much as your website. It feeds the map results. Keep the name, address, phone number and hours identical everywhere they appear. We cover it step by step in a Google Business Profile for a taproom.

Write pages that answer real questions in your own voice: what a style tastes like, how your taproom works, what to expect on a tour. Do not copy text from other sites. Do not publish thin pages made only to catch searches. Fewer, better pages beat many weak ones. See content that brings visitors to a drinks website.

Alcohol marketing is regulated. The rules differ by country and in India by state. Do not aim content at under-age people, do not suggest drinking more and follow local advertising rules. Include a clear responsible drinking line. Add an age statement where required. Check with a lawyer or the regulator if unsure.

Week one: list every page on your site and fix the titles, descriptions and contact details. Week two: claim and complete your Business Profile. Week three: add or rewrite the pages for your core beers and your taproom visit. Week four: set up Search Console and a simple count of bookings and enquiries, then note the starting figures.

After that, add a useful page or two each month and review the numbers each quarter. Keep a changes log with dates, because when something moves you will want to know what you did just before.

A word on cost: most of this takes time and care, not money. Where a developer is needed, it is usually for speed, mobile layout and the age gate. A short job can fix them. The point is to build habits you can keep, because search results reward sites that stay accurate and useful over years.
How to tell if it is working

Use Search Console to see which searches show your site and which clicks you get. Use your booking and enquiry counts to see whether visits turn into action. Look at trends over months, since results are slow and can shift. Set up simple tracking before you start so that you have a baseline. We cover this in measuring website leads.
faqs: There is no fixed time. Improvements to a small site can be noticed within weeks or take months. Nobody can promise a result. Measure over quarters, not days.
Do I need an SEO agency?
Not necessarily. A small brewery can do the basics itself. An adviser helps if the site is technically broken or you have many pages.
Is social media a substitute for SEO?
No. Social media reaches people who follow you. Search reaches people who are looking right now.
